edits.text: When judging Contra risk, consider the whole remainder of the sentence, not just the immediate right fragment. Ask: could any later clause or phrase anywhere after this cut, when taken on its own, make the already-heard left fragment false, reversed, or misleading? If any downstream material can overturn the left fragment, raise the contra probability accordingly. In short: contra = the probability that any later material in the sentence, taken alone, would contradict or negate the left-side fragment.

Treat functionally open left fragments as inherently low-cohesion. If the left side ends with a clause-opener/subordinator, an auxiliary or negation that requires a following verb phrase, a predicate missing its object or complement, or a modifier/title that attaches forward to a later head (e.g. role + name, adjective + noun, a preposition expecting its object), assign a reduced cohesion score. Concretely ask: can the left fragment stand as a sensible, self-contained assertion when translated and played now? If not, lower cohesion.

Keep these as semantic judgements you can apply at every boundary: assess whether the right-hand fragment can (1) contradict or negate the already-heard left fragment and (2) stand alone when translated without leaving essential relations unresolved. If any downstream material can do so, raise the contra probability accordingly.
